newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries open lower, rate jitters prevail.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries open lower, rate jitters prevail.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices opened lower on Monday with the market unable to shake off its fears that the Federal Reserve will soon raise interest rates.

The Fed's policy-making Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meets next week on March 25 and the market is split over whether the Fed will raise rates at that time. The economy has seen no inflation at the wholesale level this year but some policymakers and analysts argue that the Fed must be "pre-emptive" in its inflation fight and move rates higher even if official inflation indicators are subdued.

"When people think about it, they recognize that it's the demand side that's probably more important to the Fed and to the future of the bond market than the ongoing low inflation numbers," said Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at I.D.E.A. "We need to see some slowing down in some of the important demand side economic releases."
Stiles said bond prices have gone down so far so fast "that it gets to the point where it can't go down more until it moves sideways for a while."
But early on Monday, the pressure was still on bond prices, he noted.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was down 9/32 to 95-23/32 in early trade, yielding 6.97 percent.
"The bond's getting close to seven percent," said Stiles. "You should see some support there."
The market gets no government economic data on Monday but Stiles said the home builders survey due this afternoon will help economists to refine their estimates for various housing indicators.

"Housing is one of the sectors (of the economy) that has refused to die," said Stiles. "We get (February) housing starts (on Tuesday) and people will be looking at this home builders' survey to get a final gauge on that."
The Treasury will sell $23.0 billion in three- and six-week bills at its weekly bill auction, a sale that is expected to be routine.
Supply will move a little more to the front of investors' minds later this week when the Treasury announces terms of its monthly two- and five-year note sale, Stiles said.
A weak dollar also weighed on the Treasury market, analysts said. The dollar weakened against the mark in early dealings in New York but was steady against the yen.

The market will also watch the February Consumer Price Index (CPI) report, due Wednesday, analysts said. The consensus forecast is for both the total CPI and the core CPI (the index with its more volatile food and energy components) each to be up 0.2 percent.
At the short end of the maturity range, three-month bill rates were up one basis point to 5.11 percent in early trade. Six-month rates were up two basis points to 5.22 percent.
The two-year note was down 1/32 to 99-14/32, yielding 6.18 percent while the three-year note was down 2/32 to 98-23/32 to yield 6.36 percent.
The five-year note was down 4/32 to 98-24/32 to yield 6.55 percent, with the 10-year note down 7/32 to 96-19/32 to yield 6.73 percent.
